case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Dowell v. Montana Department of Public Health & Human Services
key_cases.holding: DPHHS's delay in providing substantiation notice and a fair hearing did not violate due process because, unlike the child-support scheme in Connell, no statute or rule imposes deadlines on the substantiation process, and collateral estoppel barred the parent from relitigating in the administrative hearing the facts she had already admitted in the district court abuse and neglect case.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Montana authority on challenging a substantiated finding — the fair-hearing process has no statutory deadlines, and admissions made in the district court case preclude relitigation.
key_cases.quote: Unlike Connell, there are no statutes or administrative rules setting forth deadlines within which DPHHS must issue substantiation notifications, conduct informal reviews, set hearings, or issue decisions.

key_cases.holding: The district court did not err in finding the child a youth in need of care; the State's burden at adjudication is proof by a preponderance of the evidence that the child has been abused, neglected or abandoned.
key_cases.relevance: This is the crisp Montana statement of the burden and standard that govern the judicial counterpart of a substantiated finding.
key_cases.quote: the State must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the child has been abused, neglected or abandoned

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; the form of the petition did not preclude the district court from adjudicating the children youths in need of care when it did, and the findings established abuse or neglect by a preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It states the elements and quantum of proof that convert an agency allegation into a judicial finding of abuse or neglect.
key_cases.quote: For a court to adjudicate a child a youth in need of care, the State must present evidence sufficient to establish that the child has been abused, neglected, or abandoned.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: a youth-in-need-of-care adjudication must precede termination, the statutory definition reaches a child in danger of abuse or neglect and not only one actually abused, and the father's treatment plans satisfied § 41-3-443(2).
key_cases.relevance: It holds that the statutory abuse/neglect definition reaches prospective as well as actual harm, which is the substantive content of a Montana founded finding.
key_cases.quote: Before terminating parental rights, the district court must first adjudicate the child as a “Youth in Need of Care.”

key_cases.case_name: Connell v. State, Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
key_cases.holding: Reversed and remanded with directions to dismiss with prejudice: where the agency failed to act within the time frames fixed by statute, administrative rule and the hearings officer, a 44-month delay in issuing a decision after the administrative hearing was undue delay that violated the party's due-process rights under Article II, Section 17 of the Montana Constitution.
key_cases.relevance: Dowell's holding that no deadlines govern DPHHS substantiation is unintelligible without this case: the difference Dowell draws is precisely that the child-protection substantiation and fair-hearing process has no statutory or regulatory timetable at all.
key_cases.quote: CSED failed to act within the time frames established by law, by administrative rule, and by the hearings officer.
